name: Ebira
world_status: statement found in an open source

earlier_scan.source_named: Scholz, Hans-Juergen 1976. Igbira phonology (SIL/UTA); also Rotifa 1982, A phonological analysis of Ebira. Neither located online.

new_statements.quote: Loan words assimilated into Ebira conform to the syllable structure of the language. Ebira has no stressed syllables like English. VV sequences with high tone followed by low tone occur where there is a stressed syllable in the English words that enter the language. [...] Ebira is an open syllable language. [p. 52] — It can be observed from the above that Ebira has three level tones and two kinetic tones. Lexical tone is directly related to the syllable structure as stated in 2.1. Every syllable has a tonal feature as one of its phonological components. [p. 86]
new_statements.citation: Adive, John Raji (1984). A descriptive study of the verbal piece in Ebira (a language of Kwara State of Nigeria). PhD thesis, University of London (SOAS). DOI 10.25501/soas.00028982.
new_statements.locator: p. 52 (PDF page 53), Chapter 2 Phonology, §2.2.4 'Loan Words in Ebira'; tone system §2.6 p. 86 (PDF p. 87). Page image saved; scanned in.
new_statements.reading: no word stress according to the source
new_statements.rule_in_words: Ebira is a register-tone language (three level tones H/M/L, plus high-falling and low-rising kinetic tones and downstep; every syllable bears a tone) and, per the author (a native speaker), has no stressed syllables; the only stress-related effect is that the stressed syllable of an English loanword is mapped onto a VV sequence with H followed by L tone (e.g. John > Ijoonu, police > iporiisi).
new_statements.exceptions: None for native words; the remark is made in the loanword section, where English stress is re-encoded as a HL tone sequence on a geminate vowel.
new_statements.domain_note: Word-level phonology (syllable structure and lexical tone); the stress remark is a passing statement in the loanword section rather than a dedicated suprasegmental analysis, and is phrased comparatively ('no stressed syllables like English'). Author describes his own speech (Obehira, Okene area).
new_statements.identity_note: Adive 1984 describes the author's own speech from Obehira in the Okene area, i.e. the main Ebira (Ebira Tao / Okene) dialect that ebir1243 covers; Scholz 1976 ('Igbira') and Ladefoged 1964 ('Igbirra') use older spellings for the same Okene-area variety. Rolle 2022 notes that nearly all Ebira literature concerns this Okene dialect; the Igu/Opanda/Ebira-Nya (Koto) varieties to the north-east are not described here.

sources.note: Ch. 2 Phonology. p. 52 (§2.2.4 Loan Words): 'Ebira has no stressed syllables like English'; English stressed syllables are rendered as VV sequences with H followed by L tone. §2.6 Tone (pp. 86-91): three level tones H/M/L, two kinetic tones (high-falling, low-rising), downstep; every syllable carries a tone. No other stress/accent statement (text layer is scrambled; pp. 52-54 and 86-87 scanned and p. 52 image read).

sources.citation: Isiaka, Adeiza Lasisi (2017). Ebira English in Nigerian supersystems: inventory and variation. PhD dissertation, TU Chemnitz, 239 pp.
sources.note: Ebira L1 sketch pp. 22-24 (9 vowels/ATR, three contrastive tones, tonal spread, geminate vowel sequences, citing Adive 1989: 12-18). All stress discussion concerns Nigerian English rhythm (syllable-timed vs stress-timed), not Ebira itself.

sources.citation: Rolle, Nicholas (2022). Unpacking portmanteaux: Non-linear morphology in the Ebira STAMP system. Studies in African Linguistics 51(1): 140-179. DOI 10.32473/sal.v51i1.124229.
sources.note: Phonology sketch pp. 143-145 (based on Scholz 1976 and Adive 1989): consonants, 9-vowel ATR harmony, three tone heights H M L plus HL and LH contours, Scholz's super-high realisation of HL, surface long vowels as VV strings. Nothing on stress or accent (the only 'accent' hits are tone diacritics).

sources.citation: Adeniyi, Kolawole (2017). The limits of perception in the tonal orthographies of three-tone systems. Linguistik Online 84(5). DOI 10.13092/lo.84.3844.
sources.note: §2.1 Ebira: 19 consonants, 9 vowels with ATR harmony, three contrastive tones H M L plus phonetic rising/falling contours, downdrift, 'total' downstep (DSH and DSM realised below M). Nothing on stress.

sources.citation: Ladefoged, Peter (1964). Igbirra notes and word-list. Journal of West African Languages 1(1): 27-37.
sources.note: Image-only scan, scanned. 'Phonology' section: 20 consonants, 9 vowels in two harmony sets, three lexical tones (high, mid, low), a vowel-length feature, tentative notes on grammatical tone with pitch tracings. No statement on stress ('I must stress that...' is the only hit).
